indistinct

in-dih-STINKT -- stress on the third syllable, STINKT. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Indistinct is not clear or sharply defined.

Only an indistinct hum reached us through the wall -- voices, perhaps, or a television left on somewhere.

Example

A photographer shoots a hummingbird at too slow a shutter speed. In the print, the bird's head is crisp, but its wings are indistinct -- a gray smear with no edge anywhere.

The camera could not pin the motion down into anything clear or sharply defined. Indistinct fits anything the senses cannot capture cleanly -- a shape in fog, a mumbled word, a memory from very early childhood.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

blurry: Blurry is a word for the eyes only: edges smear, outlines melt, a photo taken with shaky hands. Indistinct covers every sense -- a shape can be indistinct, but so can a mumbled word or a half-remembered voice that no eye ever saw.

vague: Vague belongs to ideas -- a vague plan or a vague promise is missing detail, not sharpness. Indistinct belongs to the senses: an indistinct sound or shape is really there in front of you, but the ear or the eye cannot pin it down.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

distinct: clearly defined and easy to make out

vivid: strikingly clear and sharp

Where it sits · how weakly it reaches the senses

hazy → indistinct → faint

hazy vs. indistinct: Hazy is a milder blur than indistinct -- a hazy skyline is softened, as if seen through thin gauze, yet you can still trace its shape, while an indistinct one cannot be made out at all.

faint vs. indistinct: Faint pushes past indistinct in its own direction: an indistinct sound is unclear in shape, while a faint one is barely there at all, so weak you may never catch it in the first place.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — in-: not (Latin in-)

root — distinct: clearly marked off and separate (Latin distinguere 'to separate, to mark apart')

Put it together: Indistinct is one of the easy ones: this unit's prefix in- ('not') plus distinct, a complete English word on its own. Latin distinguere meant 'to mark apart,' so distinct things can be told one from another -- and indistinct things cannot, because their edges never separate from what surrounds them.

Use the root in a new word: distinguish: The judges had one afternoon to distinguish among forty science-fair entries.

Root Check

Word Choice

Indistinct describes what the senses cannot pin down: an indistinct shape, an indistinct murmur, indistinct handwriting, an indistinct memory. When the thing that is unclear is an idea rather than a sight or a sound, English usually reaches for vague instead.
